doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
title: How important lyrics are to a jazz musician
summary: Walton says lyrics are very important and cites Lester Young's advice to learn them, admitting he knows only the most important words of each song.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You also, going back to your mother, she'd go along and she'd play things. She would sing the songs, so she knew the words.
The words were on the sheet music.
Well, how much important, how important, to you, are words that go along … the lyrics to songs that you play?

I think the words, I'd say very, very important. I love words but I, I'm guilty of not being a complete, I think, student of, of all words like a few artists I've heard that uh, recommended that like Lester Young, I believe. One great artist, uh, insisted that the musician,

uh, learn the lyrics to the pieces that they decide to play, if they had words, and that was important to their performance. And so I'm guilty of only half doing that. I know the, I think, the most important words in a piece, but I'm guilty of not knowing the complete, uh, uh, lyric. And so uh, um, guilty as charged. I mean, even though you didn't charge me, I don't think. [laughs]
[laughs] Okay. I'm trying to defend myself as well as I can, yeah.
[laughs] Can I have some of this water?
